content:
In Numbers chapter twelve, Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because he had married a Cushite woman. On the surface, their complaint was about Moses' marriage. But Yahweh revealed that the real issue was far deeper.

They said, "Has the LORD spoken only through Moses? Hasn't he spoken through us, too?" (Numbers 12:2). Their words about his wife were only the covering. The hidden matter underneath was jealousy, position, and ambition. Today we begin to draw out the spiritual lessons of this for us, the New Creation.

This is a very serious lesson. Sometimes Yahweh blesses a brother or sister.
He gives them a work, or grace, or understanding, or opportunity, or He uses them in a special service. And instead of rejoicing, jealousy can slowly begin to rise in the heart. But because jealousy looks ugly when it is seen plainly, the human heart often dresses it in another garment. We may say, "I am only concerned about the work." We may say, "I am only speaking for the truth."We may say, "I am only pointing out a weakness." But Yahweh sees whether the real root is bitterness, envy, or wounded pride. James warns us clearly,"But if you are bitterly jealous and there is selfish ambition in your heart, don't cover up the truth with boasting and lying" (James 3:14).

This is exactly what happened in Numbers twelve. Miriam and Aaron covered the truth. Their outward subject was Moses' wife, but their inward problem was, "Why only Moses? Has Yahweh not spoken through us also?" Jealousy often speaks this way. It does not usually announce itself and say, "I am jealous." Instead it may say, "Why is he being used?" "Why is she being appreciated?" "Why was I not asked?" "Why did they choose that family?"

"Why is their child blessed?" "Why is that brother preaching?" "Why is that sister respected?" "Why are their prayers answered?" "Why are they growing while I am overlooked?" These questions may sound reasonable, but underneath them may be a heart that is quietly bitter.

This is why we must examine our hearts before Yahweh, for the heart can deceive us. Jeremiah 17:9 says, "The human heart is the most deceitful of all things, and desperately wicked. Who really knows how bad it is?" We may think our complaint is pure, but Yahweh may see a hidden root. Hebrews 12:15 warns, "Watch out that no poisonous root of bitterness grows up to trouble you, corrupting many." Bitterness never stays private. Miriam's complaint affected Aaron also, and their words brought the whole camp to a stop. In the same way, jealousy in one heart can spread to another heart. One person's bitterness can become a family issue, a group issue, or even a congregation issue. It can delay the journey of the whole flock.

We must also remember that Yahweh has called and anointed His people for service. In the Greek, the word for anointed comes from christos. In the Greek Old Testament of Psalm 105:15, where it says, "Touch not mine anointed," the word is from christos, meaning anointed ones. So when we speak against Yahweh's servants out of jealousy and bitterness, we must be very careful.

We are not speaking against ordinary people only. We may be touching those whom Yahweh Himself has set apart for His purpose. Psalm 105:15 says,"Do not touch my chosen people, and do not hurt my prophets." Now this does not mean that no servant can ever be corrected. If there is real sin, it must be dealt with according to Scripture. But it does mean that we must not attack, accuse, or criticize from jealousy, ambition, or pride. Miriam and Aaron thought they were simply speaking about Moses, but Yahweh took the matter very seriously, because Moses was His appointed servant.

And this is where Yahweh's own words should make every one of us stop and tremble. He did not treat their complaint as a small family disagreement.

He asked them a question so piercing that it still searches our hearts today whenever we are about to speak against another. Before we open our mouths about a brother, a sister, an elder, a servant, or a worker in the flock, that same question waits to be answered. What was the question Yahweh asked, and how should it change the way we speak about one another? That is where we will continue tomorrow.

O Yahweh, our Father,

Search our hearts and show us any jealousy we have dressed in spiritual words.

We confess that our hearts can deceive us, calling envy 'concern' and bitterness 'truth.'

Help us to rejoice when You bless our brothers and sisters, and not to envy their portion.

Guard us from speaking against those whom You have anointed for Your own purpose.

Pull out every poisonous root of bitterness before it grows and corrupts many.

"Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts." - Psalm 139:23

In the name of Christ, we pray. Amen.
